questions.question: In the lecture's `Student` class, `college` is declared as `static String college = "IIT Guwahati";`. What does `static` change?
options: Each Student object gets its own copy of `college`, but the value can never change
There is a single copy of `college` that belongs to the class and is shared by all Student objects, accessed as `Student.college`
`college` can only be read inside the constructor
`college` becomes a local variable of `main`
questions.explanation: A static field is a class variable: one copy shared by every object, accessed with `ClassName.variable`. That saves storing the same college in every Student. Making a value unchangeable is the job of `final`, not `static`, which is the mix-up in the first option.

questions.question: The program is started with `java Demo5 input.txt output.txt`. What does it print?
options:
Number of arguments are 3
Argument 0 = Demo5
Argument 1 = input.txt
Argument 2 = output.txt

Number of arguments are 2
Argument 1 = input.txt
Argument 2 = output.txt
Number of arguments are 0

Number of arguments are 2
Argument 0 = input.txt
Argument 1 = output.txt
questions.explanation: The words after the class name are passed to `main` as the `String[] args` array, starting at index 0, so args = {"input.txt", "output.txt"}. Unlike C, Java does not put the program/class name in `args[0]`. Running just `java Demo5` would give length 0.

questions.question: In Demo4, `final int x; x = 4;` compiles fine. A teammate then adds `x = 5;` on the next line. What happens?
options: Compile error: a final variable can be assigned only once
It compiles and x becomes 5, because the first assignment was not at the declaration
It compiles, but throws an exception at run time on `x = 5`
It compiles and x silently stays 4
questions.explanation: A final variable may be left blank at declaration, as in Demo4, but it can be assigned exactly once; a second assignment is rejected by the compiler. This is what makes final suitable for constants such as PI. Nothing is deferred to run time and nothing is silently ignored.

questions.question: The lecture's comment asks "why is main static?" What is the reason?
options: So that `main` can access every instance variable of the class directly
Because static methods run faster than instance methods
So the JVM can call it as `Demo4.main(args)` without first creating an object of `Demo4`
Because a class can contain only one static method, and it must be `main`
questions.explanation: Static methods belong to the class, so the JVM can invoke `ClassName.main(args)` at startup without needing `new Demo4()` first. Being static actually prevents `main` from touching instance variables directly. Classes may have any number of static methods, and speed is not the reason.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: Rohit IIT Guwahati IIT Guwahati
Rohit IIT Guwahati IIT Delhi
Rohit IIT Delhi IIT Delhi
Compile error: a static variable cannot be accessed through `s1`
questions.explanation: There is only one `college` variable, owned by the class; `s1.college` is just another (discouraged) way of writing `Student.college`. So the assignment changes the shared value seen through `s2` and `Student` alike. Accessing a static through a reference compiles (with a warning), so it is not an error.

questions.question: Which marked line fails to compile?
options: Line 1: a static method cannot print a variable
Line 2: a static method has no `this`, so it cannot reach the instance variable `name`
Line 3: an instance method cannot read a static variable
Line 4: an instance method cannot call a static method
questions.explanation: The lecture's rules say a static method can directly use only static members and has no access to `this`, because it is not called on any object. The restrictions apply only in that direction: instance methods like `print()` may freely use static variables and call static methods, so lines 3 and 4 are fine.

questions.question: The `Random` class has `static final double PI;` and a static block `static { PI = 3.14; }`. When does that static block run?
options: Once, when the class is loaded and initialized, before it is first used; not again for each new object
Every time `new Random()` is called, just before the constructor
Only when a method explicitly calls it by name
At compile time, so it never runs while the program executes
questions.explanation: A static block runs a single time when the class is initialized, which makes it the place to set static fields such as a blank `static final` constant or `grade = 8` in Demo.java. Code that should run for every object belongs in a constructor instead. Static blocks have no name, so they cannot be called explicitly.

questions.question: The notes say a static method can only call other static methods. A teammate's `main` (static) needs to call the instance method `markAttendance()` of `Student`. Which approach compiles and works?
options: Call `markAttendance();` directly inside `main`
Call `this.markAttendance();` inside `main`
Call `Student.markAttendance();` from `main`
Create an object first, e.g. `Student s1 = new Student(...); s1.markAttendance();`
questions.explanation: The rule means a static method cannot call instance members directly, because there is no current object. With an explicit object reference, any static method (including `main`) can call instance methods, which is exactly what all the lecture demos do. `this` does not exist in static context, and `ClassName.method()` works only for static methods.

questions.question: What is the exact output?
questions.explanation: `Counter` is initialized when it is first used (the first `new Counter()`), so "M " prints before "S ", and the static block runs only once. Each constructor increments the shared `count` (11, then 12) and stores it in its own instance field `id`, so a.id stays 11 while Counter.count is 12. '12 12' would require `id` to be static too.

questions.question: A teammate declares `final Random r = new Random(4, 5);` (Random has int fields `x`, `y`) and expects it to be fully read-only. Which statement about the next lines is correct?
options: `r.x = 10;` compiles and changes the object, but `r = new Random(1, 2);` is a compile error
Both `r.x = 10;` and `r = new Random(1, 2);` are compile errors, because the whole object is frozen
`r.x = 10;` is a compile error, but `r = new Random(1, 2);` is allowed once
Both lines compile, because final applies only to primitive variables
questions.explanation: `final` on a reference variable fixes the reference: `r` must always point to the same object, so reassigning it fails to compile. It does not make the object's fields final, so `r.x = 10` is allowed. To make the data unchangeable, the fields `x` and `y` themselves would have to be final.
